Date: 2026-04-29
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Tom Reynolds (Citrine Head of Platform), Aisha Khan (Citrine ML Eng), Eric Soto (Citrine Security)
summary: Redwood ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on lookahead/prefix KV caching and batching strategies to reduce token cost for Citrine's multi-turn product Q&A workload. Discussed console recommendations, prefetch heuristics, TTLs, sessionization, and tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated deployment. Security and SSO/KMS questions surfaced; agreed on a 2-week POC and a benchmark session next week.
topics: KV prefix lookahead and prefetch heuristics
batch sizing and latency vs cost tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE. Quick intros?
[00:08] Tom Reynolds: Tom here, Head of Platform at Citrine. We'll be focusing on production costs for our Q&A flows.
[00:15] Aisha Khan: Aisha, ML eng, I own inference infra and budgets.
[00:19] Eric Soto: Eric, security lead—I'll ask the usual SOC2/KMS questions.
[00:24] Maya Chen: Hey team, Maya from Redwood SE, I'll walk the Optimize console and run through lookahead / prefix cache recs.
[00:31] Jordan Lee: Cool. Goal for today: show specific batching + KV prefetch patterns to cut per-token spend and put numbers on potential savings for your traffic profile.
[00:41] Tom Reynolds: High level, our 95th percentile lat target is 300ms, but cost is creeping up. We need a path to 30-40% savings ideally.
[00:49] Maya Chen: Got it. Could you share rough numbers: average session length, concurrent sessions, and typical prompt prefix sizes?
[00:56] Aisha Khan: Average session about 6 turns, prefix ~120 tokens, concurrency ~250 peak, baseline tps ~35.
[01:04] Maya Chen: Perfect. So first concept: prefix KV caching with lookahead prefetch. Instead of caching only exact prefix hits, we prefetch likely next KV pages based on session history—this lifts hit rate for multi-turn flows.
[01:20] Tom Reynolds: When you say prefetch, is that synchronous on the request path? Concerned about added latency.
[01:26] Maya Chen: Good question. Our recommendation is async lookahead that primes the KV in the background for sessions with high probability of follow-on tokens. For high-latency-sensitive endpoints we use a hybrid: synchronous for first few tokens, async thereafter.
[01:36] Jordan Lee: And the Optimize console will simulate hit-rate uplift for your distribution; we'll show you modeled savings.
[01:42] [01:45] Speaker 1: mhm, okay.
[01:48] Maya Chen: I'll demo the console now. On the Optimize > Prefetch tab you can upload traces or link a streaming parquet—
[01:53] Aisha Khan: We can provide traces—some obfuscation required, but we can export session-level token traces.
[01:59] Maya Chen: Great. Loading the Citrine sample trace... okay the model predicts a baseline cache hit of 12% with naive prefix caching, lookahead prefetch increases that to ~38% for your sample.
[02:10] Tom Reynolds: That's a big jump. Is that consistent across different user cohorts?
[02:14] Maya Chen: Depends—short sessions have less lift, long multi-turn sessions benefit more. Our console breaks it down by session length.
[02:21] Jordan Lee: On cost numbers: with your baseline throughput the model projects 28% token cost reduction at 30% hit rate, up to 45% if we can reach 50% hit rate with combined batching and prefetch.
[02:33] Eric Soto: What's the memory footprint of storing the prefetched KV entries? Any concerns for data leakage or PII?
[02:39] Maya Chen: The KV entries are bounded by TTL and cached only in encrypted memory. For PII we recommend field-level token redaction before caching and also configuring cache namespaces per customer.
[02:50] Eric Soto: And KMS?
[02:53] Jordan Lee: Redwood supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). We'll share our KMS integration docs.
[02:58] [03:00] Speaker 2: right, right.
[03:02] Maya Chen: Next, batching: continuous batching inside the runtime reduces per-token CPU/GPU overhead. The console suggests batch sizes to hit your latency SLOs—so you don't over-batch.
[03:13] Aisha Khan: What batch sizes are we talking about at 250 concurrency?
[03:17] Maya Chen: For your trace, recommended dynamic batch target of 16–24 tokens per step, adaptive based on measured quantiles. That gave us median latency ~220ms in our sim.
[03:26] Tom Reynolds: Are those numbers assuming hosted or dedicated?
[03:29] Maya Chen: Good catch—numbers vary. The sim default is hosted with our high-throughput runtime; dedicated GPUs will shift the cost curve, typically lower per-token compute cost but you add reserved capacity overhead. Console shows both scenarios.
[03:40] Jordan Lee: For Citrine, based on usage, the tipping point for dedicated vs hosted looks around sustained 80M tokens/month, which from Aisha's numbers you might approach if adoption grows.
[03:51] Aisha Khan: Hmm okay. We expect seasonal spikes too. How does auto-burst work?
[03:55] Maya Chen: Dedicated has burst lanes to handle spikes; Optimize can suggest buffer sizing to avoid overprovisioning.
[04:02] Tom Reynolds: Walk me through an example config we could use in our canary.
[04:06] Maya Chen: Sure—canary profile: enable prefix KV with lookahead depth=2, TTL=10m for session cache, prefetch throttling at 20qps per instance, adaptive batch target 18. Use session affinity for the first 30s to increase hit continuity.
[04:19] Aisha Khan: If TTL=10m, what's eviction behavior under memory pressure?
[04:24] Maya Chen: LRU with priority hints—we suggest pinning active sessions and evicting larger, older prefixes. Console tunables include evict-on-memory-pct and pin-thresholds.
[04:34] [04:36] Speaker 3: hmm.
[04:38] Eric Soto: For compliance we need audit logs for cache access—any way to surface that?
[04:42] Jordan Lee: Yes, the Private offering streams audit logs to your SIEM and includes per-request cache trace metadata. We'll add a sample log format.
[04:50] Maya Chen: Also, for your PII workflows, we can scope a redaction preprocessor in the ingestion pipeline—works with our SDKs.
[04:58] Tom Reynolds: On the savings spreadsheet—how conservative is it? I worry about overpromising.
[05:03] Jordan Lee: The spreadsheet has baseline/optimistic/conservative tabs. Our conservative numbers assume 20% lower hit uplift and 10% added tail latency. We also include sensitivity to TTL and batch size.
[05:16] Aisha Khan: Any downside—model quality regressions? If caching returns stale context could responses degrade.
[05:21] Maya Chen: There's a small profile-dependent risk. We recommend coupling caching changes with prompt sets in Redwood's evals harness—automated regression alerts.
[05:30] Tom Reynolds: Could we see a live demo of a POC run from the console?
[05:33] Maya Chen: Yes—quick demo. I'll open the POC workspace, click "New Savings Sandbox," attach your sample trace, choose lookahead depth 2, TTL 10m, and run sim.
[05:44] [05:46] Speaker 1: okay.
[05:47] Maya Chen: Sim running... estimating 45s for full sim on your trace. While that's running, a couple of sec on orchestration: routing policies can send beta traffic to a cheaper model variant automatically if cost crosses threshold, with automatic fallback.
[05:59] Tom Reynolds: We have internal model variants—do you support model routing based on tag and latency?
[06:04] Jordan Lee: Yep—you can route by tag, region, and latency SLO; Optimize suggests thresholds.
[06:09] Maya Chen: Sim results are in: projected 33% token cost reduction conservative, 43% optimistic. Hit rate uplift broken down by session length attached in the console.
[06:19] Aisha Khan: Nice. Can you share the sim output CSV?
[06:22] Maya Chen: I'll export and share after the call.
[06:25] Eric Soto: Security recap: we'll need SOC2 docs, KMS key exchange, support for SAML 2.0, and an options matrix for VPC or private deployment.
[06:34] Jordan Lee: We'll send all three: SOC2 report, KMS integration guide, and a Private deployment checklist.
[06:40] Tom Reynolds: Good. On commercial: what's short POC pricing look like?
[06:44] Jordan Lee: For a 2-week POC we can offer a usage credit plus an evaluation rate—I'll include numbers in the spreadsheet.
[06:50] Maya Chen: Also we'll include a sample airflow for how prefetch jobs run and a sample mem footprint calculation for your instance types.
[06:58] Aisha Khan: One more: do you have a recommended quantization profile to pair with caching?
[07:02] Maya Chen: Yes, quant32 or int8 dynamic depending on model family; Optimize will recommend profiles with expected latency and quality delta.
[07:10] Tom Reynolds: OK let's recap next steps.
[07:12] Jordan Lee: Action items: Jordan send cost model + POC pricing, Maya run baseline perf with your traces and export sim CSV, Tom to confirm POC stakeholders and infra. We'll schedule the 90m benchmark for next Tuesday 10am PT.
[07:27] Tom Reynolds: That works for us. Thanks both.
[07:30] Jordan Lee: Thanks all—we'll also include the SOC2 and KMS docs in the follow-up email.
[07:35] Aisha Khan: Appreciate it. bye.
[07:37] [07:40] End of recording.
